The 3 Fundamental Rules of Electric Circuits

Rule 1: The Water Pipe Analogy

Think of electricity as water circulating in pipes:
• Voltage (V): The water pressure created by a pump (the electric cell).
• Current (I): The rate of water flow in litres/sec (coulombs of charge per sec, I = Q/t).
• Resistance (R): A narrow pipe constriction that resists water flow.

Key Insight: Without water pressure (voltage), zero water flows! A dead battery has 0V pressure.

Rule 2: The Continuous Closed Loop

Electric current can ONLY flow in an unbroken loop. If there is a gap anywhere in the circuit—a loose screw, an open switch, or a snapped wire—current stops instantly everywhere in the entire circuit!

Circuit Terminology: Switch ON = Closed circuit (Bulb glows) | Switch OFF = Open circuit (Air gap stops current).

Rule 3: Conventional vs Electron Current

Conventional Current: By historical scientific tradition, current is drawn flowing from Positive (+) to Negative (-).

Electron Flow: In reality, negative electrons are repelled from the negative terminal and drift towards positive!

Board Exam Rule: Always draw circuit current arrows going from (+) to (-)!
2

The Anatomy of Cells, Batteries & Bulbs

Power Source Polarity Rule

Electric Cell vs. Battery

An electric cell has two terminals:
• Positive terminal (+): The raised metallic cap.
• Negative terminal (-): The flat metallic disc at the base.

How to Connect a Battery (Series Connection):

A battery is a combination of two or more cells. To make them work together, connect the positive terminal of one cell to the negative terminal of the next!

⚠️ Common Mistake: Connecting (+) to (+) or (-) to (-) causes the voltages to fight each other (1.5 V − 1.5 V = 0 V), and the bulb will NEVER glow!
Light Emitter Tungsten Filament

Anatomy of an Electric Bulb (Eidetic Memory Visual)

Inside a glass bulb is a tiny coiled wire called the filament, made of pure Tungsten (melting point 3422°C). The filament is supported by two thick lead-in wires.

Why Does a "Fused" Bulb Never Glow?

When excessive current or age causes the thin tungsten wire to snap, the bulb is said to be fused.

Snapped Filament ➔ Air Gap inside Bulb ➔ Open Circuit ➔ 0 Amperes Current Everywhere!

Schematic Representation

Circuit Elements & Standardized Symbols

Mastering official NCERT schematic symbols, drawing conventions, and component polarities.

Component 1 NCERT Essential

Electric Cell

Represented by two parallel vertical lines:
• The longer, thinner line represents the Positive terminal (+).
• The shorter, thicker line represents the Negative terminal (-).

Component 2 Series Assembly

Electric Battery

A combination of two or more cells joined in series. Alternating long-thin and short-thick lines show positive connected to negative in daisy-chain succession.

Component 3 Closed Key

Switch in 'ON' Position

Both terminal dots are bridged solidly by a straight horizontal conducting bar. Circuit is complete and closed; current flows freely.

Component 4 Open Key

Switch in 'OFF' Position

The conducting bridge is lifted up, creating an air gap between terminal dots. The circuit is open; resistance is infinite and current is zero.

Component 5 Filament Lamp

Electric Bulb (Lamp)

A circle containing a cursive curly loop representing the tungsten filament. When glowing, radiating dashes or a glowing halo are drawn around it.

Component 6 Conductor

Connecting Wire

A straight continuous line representing insulated copper or aluminium wire with negligible resistance, providing an unbroken conduction path.

Why Do We Use Schematic Circuit Diagrams Instead of Realistic Pictures?

1. Universal Standardization

Realistic pictures vary by manufacturer and are complicated and slow to draw. Schematic symbols are internationally standardized by IUPAC and ISO, allowing any engineer or student in the world to understand the exact electrical connections instantly.

2. Clear Circuit Topology

Schematic diagrams emphasize the logical connections between nodes and components rather than physical appearance, making it effortless to trace whether loops are closed or open and detect faulty connections.

Circuit Diagnostics

Circuit Dynamics & Fault Troubleshooting

Understanding open vs closed loops, series vs parallel arrangements, and the 6 classic reasons circuits fail.

Condition: Complete Loop 💡 Bulb Glows

Closed Electric Circuit

When the switch is in the 'ON' position, the metal contacts touch, providing a continuous, unbroken path of conducting wire from the positive terminal of the cell, through the bulb, and back to the negative terminal.

• Resistance = Normal circuit load (R)
• Current Flow = Active (I > 0 Amperes)
• Energy Flow = Chemical ➔ Electrical ➔ Heat & Light
Condition: Broken Loop 🌑 Bulb Stays Dark

Open Electric Circuit

When the switch is in the 'OFF' position, or if a wire is disconnected, an air gap is created in the path. Because air is an electrical insulator, electrons cannot bridge the gap, and current immediately ceases throughout the circuit.

• Resistance = Infinite (due to air gap)
• Current Flow = Zero (I = 0 Amperes)
• Energy Flow = Zero electrical energy transmitted
!

The 6 Classic Reasons a Circuit Fails to Light the Bulb

1. Fused Bulb Filament

The delicate tungsten filament inside the glass bulb is broken. Even though the exterior wires are intact, the broken filament creates an open circuit inside the bulb itself.

2. Reversed Cell Polarity

Cells in the battery holder are placed facing the same direction (+ to + or - to -). Opposing potentials cancel each other out (1.5 V − 1.5 V = 0 V), producing zero net voltage.

3. Dead / Discharged Cell

The chemical electrolyte inside the cell is completely exhausted. The cell has 0V potential difference and can no longer push charges through the circuit.

4. Loose Connections

Wires are not twisted tightly onto terminals or screws. Even microscopic physical gaps between conductors prevent electron flow.

5. Insulation Not Stripped

Connecting wires are clamped onto the plastic/enamel coating instead of exposed shiny copper metal. The plastic insulation blocks current.

6. Accidental Short-Circuit

A wire connects the positive and negative cell terminals directly together without going through the bulb. Current takes the zero-resistance shortcut, bypassing the bulb entirely!

Series vs. Parallel Connections in Real Life

Series Circuit

Single Common Path

Components are connected one after another in a single line. The same current flows through all appliances.

⚠️ Fatal Flaw: If one bulb fuses, the entire loop breaks and ALL other appliances shut down! (e.g. cheap decorative Diwali fairy lights).
Parallel Circuit (Household Standard)

Independent Branches

Each appliance is connected across separate branches. Every branch receives the full supply voltage (220V).

✓ Huge Advantage: If a bedroom bulb fuses, the kitchen lights, fan, and refrigerator continue working completely unaffected!
Thermal Dissipation

Heating Effect of Current & Joule's Law

Lattice collisions, Joule's mathematical law (H = I²Rt), Nichrome heating elements, and the lighting paradox.

1

Why Do Wires Heat Up? The Atomic Collision Mechanism

When an electrical potential pushes free electrons through a metallic conductor, they do not travel through empty space. They continuously collide with vibrating metal ions in the lattice. Each impact transfers kinetic energy from the moving charges into heat vibration in the atoms.

Joule's Mathematical Law of Heating
H = I² · R · t
Where: H = Heat produced (Joules), I = Current (Amperes), R = Resistance (Ohms), t = Time (Seconds).
★ Exam Formula Note: Heat depends on the square of the current (I²). If you double the current (2×), the heat produced quadruples (4×)!
Element Metallurgy Nichrome Alloy

Why Nichrome is the Universal Heating Element

Appliances like room heaters, geysers, toasters, and irons use a coil of Nichrome (an alloy of Nickel + Chromium). Nichrome is chosen because of 3 unique properties:

  • High Electrical Resistance: Generates massive heat per unit length compared to copper.
  • Extremely High Melting Point: Remains solid without melting even at glowing red temperatures (> 1000°C).
  • Resistance to Oxidation: Does not react or burn in atmospheric air when red-hot.
Classic Board Exam Question

Why Do Connecting Wires Stay Cool While the Heater Element Glows Red-Hot?

Both the connecting cord and the heating element carry the exact same electrical current (I). However, the connecting wires are made of thick pure Copper which has very low resistance (Rcopper ≈ 0). By H = I²Rt, negligible heat is developed in copper. In contrast, the heating element is made of thin coiled Nichrome with huge resistance (Rnichrome ≫ Rcopper), generating enormous concentrated heat and glowing red!

Evolution of Lighting: From Tungsten Filament to Modern LEDs

💡

Traditional Filament Bulb

Contains a pure Tungsten wire filament heated to white-hot glow (2500°C) in an inert atmosphere of Argon and Nitrogen gas.

⚠️ 90% wasted as heat; only 10% converted to light. Extremely inefficient.
🌀

Compact Fluorescent Lamp (CFL)

Uses gas discharge through mercury vapor to excite a phosphor coating inside spiral glass tubes, producing far less wasted heat.

✓ ~75% less electricity consumption than filament bulbs. Contains toxic mercury.
✨

Light Emitting Diode (LED)

Semiconductor diode that releases photons directly via electron recombination. Operates completely cool to the touch with zero filaments.

★ The Champion: 85% energy savings, instant start, 25,000+ hours lifespan.
Circuit Protection

Electrical Safety: Fuses, MCBs & Fire Prevention

Understanding short-circuit surges, overloading hazards, sacrificial fuse wire alloys, and modern MCB tripping.

Hazard #1 Extreme Hazard

Short-Circuiting

Occurs when the Live wire directly touches the Neutral wire due to damaged, worn, or cracked plastic insulation.

• Circuit Resistance (R) ➔ Drops close to 0 Ω
• Current (I = V/R) ➔ Surges into hundreds of Amperes!
• Immediate Result ➔ Violent sparking and electrical fire!
Hazard #2 Overheating Hazard

Overloading

Occurs when too many high-power appliances (e.g., air conditioner, microwave, geyser, room heater) are connected simultaneously to a single electrical socket.

• Total current drawn exceeds the rated limit of the wire
• Wires become intensely hot (H = I²Rt)
• Plastic insulation melts, triggering short-circuits and fires
1

The Electric Fuse: Sacrificial Guardian

An electric fuse is a safety device inserted into an electrical circuit that protects appliances and prevents house fires by breaking the circuit whenever the current exceeds a predetermined safe limit.

Fuse Working Principle:

The fuse wire is made of a special alloy of Tin (Sn) and Lead (Pb) having a very Low Melting Point. When an overcurrent surges through the circuit, Joule heating (H = I²Rt) quickly raises the fuse wire temperature above its melting point. The wire melts and snaps, breaking the circuit in milliseconds!

Fatal Safety Hazard

Why Ordinary Copper Wire Must NEVER Be Used As a Fuse!

Some people make the dangerous mistake of wrapping ordinary copper wire around a burnt fuse cartridge. Copper has a very high melting point (1085°C)! When an electrical surge occurs, the copper wire will NOT melt. Current continues to surge unimpeded, burning out costly TV/refrigerator motors and causing domestic fires!

2

Modern MCBs (Miniature Circuit Breakers)

Modern Standard: MCB

Miniature Circuit Breakers

MCBs are automatic electromagnetic switches fitted in modern distribution boxes. When current in a branch exceeds the safe threshold, the internal electromagnet trips the switch to the 'OFF' position automatically.

★ Key Advantage: No wire replacement needed! Once you fix the faulty appliance, you simply flip the MCB lever back to 'ON' with your fingertip.
Consumer Assurance

The ISI Mark of Safety

Always check for the official ISI Mark (Bureau of Indian Standards - BIS) on electrical appliances, extension cords, fuses, and MCBs. Substandard electrical components lacking the ISI mark use impure alloys and thin insulation that lead to deadly house fires.

Electromagnetism

Magnetic Effect of Current & Oersted's Discovery

How Hans Christian Oersted proved that electric current generates a magnetic field in 1820.

1

The Accidental Discovery That Changed Modern Physics (1820)

In 1820, Danish physicist Hans Christian Oersted was lecturing to students. He noticed that whenever he completed an electric circuit, a nearby magnetic compass needle jerked and deflected away from the Earth's magnetic north!

Oersted's 3 Key Observations:
1. Current Switched ON ➔ Compass needle immediately deflects.
2. Current Switched OFF ➔ Needle swings back to natural North-South position.
3. Current Direction Reversed ➔ Needle deflects in the opposite direction!

★ The Grand Conclusion: When electric current passes through a wire, the wire behaves exactly like a magnet!

N
S
W
E
Compass Needle Deflection: A magnetic compass needle is itself a tiny pivot-mounted bar magnet. It only deflects when an external magnetic field acts on it.
Field Geometry

Concentric Circular Field Lines

The magnetic field lines surrounding a straight current-carrying wire form concentric circles centered on the wire. The field is strongest close to the wire and weakens as you move further away.

Maxwell's Rule

Right-Hand Thumb Rule

Imagine gripping the wire with your right hand with your thumb pointing in the direction of conventional current (+ to −). Your curled fingers point in the direction of the concentric magnetic field lines!

Controllable Magnetism

Electromagnets & Industrial Engineering

Coil physics, soft iron core metallurgy, magnetic strength factors, and heavy scrapyard cranes.

1

What is an Electromagnet?

An electromagnet is a magnet consisting of a coil of insulated copper wire wrapped tightly around a piece of magnetic material, typically a soft iron core. It behaves as a powerful magnet ONLY when electric current flows through the coil!

Why Use Soft Iron Instead of Steel?

• Soft Iron Core: Magnetizes instantly when current is ON, and demagnetizes completely the split-second current is switched OFF (Temporary Magnet).
• Steel Core: Once magnetized, steel retains its magnetism permanently even after current stops. An electromagnet made with steel could never be switched off!

1. Number of Turns (N)

More turns of wire wound onto the core produce a stronger magnetic field (B ∝ N).

2. Electric Current (I)

Higher current amperage pumping through the coil boosts magnetic strength (B ∝ I).

3. Core Permeability

A soft iron core multiplies magnetic flux hundreds of times compared to empty air.

4. Winding Density

Compact, tightly layered windings concentrate the magnetic poles at the ends.

Real-World Engineering Applications of Electromagnets

🏗️

Scrapyard Cranes

Massive circular electromagnets lift scrap iron, steel girders, and whole automobiles. Switch current ON to lift; switch current OFF to drop!

🚄

Maglev Bullet Trains

Superconducting electromagnets levitate high-speed trains 10 cm above tracks, eliminating wheel friction to travel at over 500 km/h.

🏥

Medical MRI Machines

Magnetic Resonance Imaging uses huge electromagnets to map internal organs and soft tissue without invasive surgical incisions.

👁️

Ophthalmic Surgery

Eye surgeons use micro-electromagnets to gently extract microscopic iron splinters accidentally lodged in a patient's eye.

Electromechanical Oscillator

The Electric Bell: Working Mechanism

Understanding the ingenious automatic make-and-break cycle that creates continuous acoustic ringing.

1

Anatomy & Key Mechanical Parts

1. U-Shaped Electromagnet

Two soft iron poles wound with insulated copper wire coils in opposite directions to form North and South poles.

2. Soft Iron Armature

A lightweight iron strip placed directly in front of the electromagnet poles, mounted on a flexible return spring.

3. Contact Screw

An adjustable brass screw whose sharp tip rests against the flexible spring attached to the armature.

4. Hammer / Striker

A small metallic sphere attached to the top end of the soft iron armature rod.

5. Metallic Gong

A resonant cup-shaped brass bowl that vibrates with a sharp ringing note when struck by the hammer.

6. Push Button & Battery

Supplies the required direct current (DC) voltage to energize the circuit when the doorbell button is held down.

2

The Continuous 6-Step "Make-and-Break" Cycle

Step 1 Push Switch

Circuit Closes

Pressing the doorbell switch completes the circuit. Electric current flows through the coil, transforming it into a powerful electromagnet.

Step 2 Magnetic Pull

Armature Attracted

The energized electromagnet exerts a strong magnetic attraction, pulling the soft iron armature towards its poles.

Step 3 DING! Sound

Hammer Strikes Gong

The striker attached to the moving armature hits the gong with a loud metallic ring.

Step 4 (Crucial!) Contact Breaks

Air Gap Created

As the armature rushes forward, it pulls away from the tip of the contact screw. This breaks the electrical contact ➔ circuit becomes OPEN!

Step 5 Demagnetization

Electromagnet Turns Off

With zero current flowing, the soft iron coil instantly loses all magnetism. It can no longer attract the armature.

Step 6 Cycle Repeats

Spring Pulls Back

The flexible return spring pulls the armature back, touching the contact screw again. The circuit closes and the entire cycle repeats 50+ times per second!

Hands-On Laboratory Suite

Activity Corner: 6 Guided Lab Investigations

Official NCERT experiential activities with step-by-step procedures, controls, observations, and safety rules.

Activity 1 • Basic Circuit NCERT 14.1

Simple Electric Circuit with Torch Bulb & Cell

Apparatus: 1.5V electric cell, torch bulb with holder, switch, insulated connecting copper wires.

Procedure: Connect the positive terminal of the cell to one terminal of the switch. Connect the other switch terminal to the bulb, and complete the loop back to the negative terminal of the cell.

• Switch in 'ON' position ➔ Bulb glows brightly (Closed Circuit).
• Switch in 'OFF' position ➔ Bulb turns dark instantly (Open Circuit).
Activity 2 • DIY Switch NCERT 14.2

Making a DIY Safety-Pin Switch

Apparatus: A small wooden board, two brass drawing pins, a metallic safety pin, wire leads.

Procedure: Insert a drawing pin through the small ring of the safety pin and fix it into the board. Fix the second drawing pin such that the free end of the safety pin can touch it easily.

• Safety pin touches 2nd drawing pin ➔ Metal bridges gap ➔ Switch ON.
• Safety pin rotated away ➔ Air gap created ➔ Switch OFF.
Activity 3 • Conductivity NCERT 14.3

Testing Conductors vs Insulators

Apparatus: Circuit with two open clip terminals A and B, various test samples.

Procedure: Connect samples across the gap and observe whether the bulb glows.

• Iron nail, key, copper coin, pencil lead ➔ Bulb glows (Conductors).
• Rubber eraser, plastic ruler, glass bangle, chalk ➔ Bulb dark (Insulators).
Activity 4 • Joule Heating NCERT 14.4

Demonstrating Heating Effect with Nichrome Wire

Apparatus: 10 cm piece of thin Nichrome wire tied between two iron nails on a wooden block, cell, switch.

Procedure: Pass current for about 10 seconds. Switch off current and gently touch the wire with a fingertip.

• Observation ➔ Nichrome wire becomes noticeably hot!
• Warning ➔ Do not touch the wire for long when high current is passing!
Activity 5 • Oersted Lab NCERT 14.5

Oersted's Compass Deflection Lab

Apparatus: Empty cardboard tray from matchbox, magnetic compass, insulated copper wire, cell, switch.

Procedure: Place compass inside tray, wrap wire several times around it, and toggle switch ON and OFF.

• Switch ON ➔ Compass needle immediately deflects from N-S alignment.
• Switch OFF ➔ Needle swings back to point North-South.
Activity 6 • Electromagnet NCERT 14.6

Building an Electromagnet with an Iron Nail

Apparatus: 8–10 cm iron nail, 1 meter of insulated copper wire, cell, switch, small steel pins.

Procedure: Wind wire tightly around nail in a neat coil. Connect ends to cell and bring pins near the tip.

• Switch ON ➔ Steel pins stick firmly to the nail tip!
• Switch OFF ➔ All pins immediately drop off (Magnetism lost).

Q1 • Short Answer Continuity Testing Across Materials
medium 2 Marks
Observe the circuit with test terminals A and B. With which of the following materials connected between the ends A and B will the lamp NOT glow? (i) Steel spoon, (ii) Plastic scale, (iii) Rubber band, (iv) Copper strip.
Model Textbook Solution
The lamp will NOT glow when a plastic scale or a rubber band is connected between terminals A and B.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Plastic and rubber are electrical insulators that possess virtually no free electrons and do not allow electric current to pass through. Steel and copper are conductors and would complete the circuit, lighting the lamp.
Q2 • Short Answer Broken Filament in Series Circuit
medium 2 Marks
In a series circuit containing two lamps, if the filament of one of the lamps is broken, will the other lamp glow? Justify your answer.
Model Textbook Solution
No, the other lamp will NOT glow. When the filament of one lamp breaks, the conducting path of the series circuit is broken, creating an open circuit with an air gap. Since electric current requires a continuous unbroken loop to flow, current stops throughout the entire circuit.
Examiner & Concept Tip: In a series circuit, current flows through a single sequential loop. A break at any point (such as a blown filament) halts current to all components.
Q3 • Short Answer Insulator Coating on Wires
easy 2 Marks
A student forgot to remove the plastic insulator covering from the ends of connecting wires while making a circuit. If the lamp and the cell are working properly, will the lamp glow? Explain.
Model Textbook Solution
No, the lamp will NOT glow. The plastic coating is an electrical insulator that does not conduct electric current. Because the insulating plastic covers the contact points, no metal-to-metal conducting contact is established with the cell and lamp terminals, leaving the circuit open.
Examiner & Concept Tip: For current to flow, electrical contact must be made directly with the internal metal conductor (copper), not the outer insulating sheath.
Q4 • Short Answer Torch Circuit Diagram with Symbols
medium 3 Marks
Draw a circuit diagram for a simple torch using standard symbols for electrical components.
Model Textbook Solution
A simple torch circuit diagram consists of:
1. Two electric cells connected in series (+ to − represented by long thin line and short thick line pairs),
2. A single-pole switch / key,
3. An electric bulb / lamp (circle with coiled filament loop),
4. Conducting connecting lines forming a closed rectangular loop.
When the switch is closed (ON), current flows from positive terminal through the bulb filament and switch back to the negative terminal.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Standard symbolic representations: Cell = ┤├ , Battery = ┤├──┤├ , Switch ON = ──•──•── , Bulb = ─(⊗)─.
Q5 • Short Answer Multi-Switch Lamp Control Circuit
medium 3 Marks
In a circuit with two switches S₁ and S₂ controlling two branch lamps L₁ and L₂: (i) If S₂ is in 'ON' position and S₁ is in 'OFF' position, which lamp(s) will glow? (ii) If S₂ is in 'OFF' position and S₁ is in 'ON' position, which lamp(s) will glow? (iii) If S₁ and S₂ both are in 'ON' position, which lamp(s) will glow? (iv) If both S₁ and S₂ are in 'OFF' position, which lamp(s) will glow?
Model Textbook Solution
(i) Only the lamp controlled by switch S₂ (L₂) will glow.
(ii) Only the lamp controlled by switch S₁ (L₁) will glow.
(iii) Both lamps (L₁ and L₂) will glow.
(iv) Neither lamp will glow.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Independent parallel branches allow each switch to control its respective branch lamp without interrupting current to the other branch.
Q6 • Short Answer Troubleshooting a Faulty Circuit
hard 4 Marks
Vidyut has made an electric circuit. Even after closing the switch, the lamp does not glow. What can be the possible reasons? List as many possible reasons as you can and describe how you would test them.
Model Textbook Solution
Possible reasons for the faulty circuit:
1. The cell or battery is completely discharged / dead.
2. The cells are connected incorrectly (e.g. positive-to-positive instead of positive-to-negative).
3. The bulb is fused (broken tungsten filament).
4. The connecting wires are loose, detached, or have broken conductors inside the insulation.
5. The switch terminals are dirty, loose, or oxidized, preventing electrical contact.
6. The insulation was not stripped from the wire ends before making connections.
Testing procedure:
- Inspect the bulb filament to see if it is intact; test with a known working cell.
- Check cell polarities and replace with fresh cells.
- Tighten all terminal connections and ensure wire ends are stripped clean.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Systematic fault isolation checks each circuit element (source, conductor, switch, and load) independently.
Q7 • Short Answer Identifying Unmarked Battery Terminals
medium 3 Marks
Suppose the '+' and '−' symbols cannot be read on a battery. Suggest a method to identify the two terminals of this battery.
Model Textbook Solution
Methods to identify the battery terminals:
Method 1 (Using an LED): Connect an LED to the battery terminals with a protective resistor. Since an LED only conducts in the forward bias direction, when the longer lead of the LED is connected to the positive terminal and the shorter lead to the negative terminal, it lights up. The terminal connected to the longer lead is the positive terminal.
Method 2 (Using a Magnetic Compass): Place a magnetic compass under a connecting wire. When connected to the battery, observe the compass needle deflection using Ampere's Right-Hand Rule or the Snow rule to determine current direction (from + to −).
Method 3 (Using a DC Voltmeter): Connect a digital multimeter/voltmeter. If the reading is positive, the red probe is on the positive terminal.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Directional electrical components (LEDs, voltmeters, magnetic needles) respond to polarity, enabling unambiguous terminal identification.
Q8 • Short Answer Designing an Activity to Test Six Cells
hard 4 Marks
You are given six cells marked A, B, C, D, E, and F. Some of these are working and some are dead. Design an activity to identify which of them are working. (i) List the items required. (ii) Write the procedure to follow. (iii) How to draw the conclusion.
Model Textbook Solution
(i) Items required: A known working low-voltage bulb (or LED with 100 Ω resistor), a bulb holder, two connecting copper wires with alligator clips, and the six test cells (A to F).
(ii) Procedure: Set up a simple test circuit consisting of the bulb connected to two free wire leads. Insert cell A between the free leads ensuring positive touches one lead and negative touches the other. Observe whether the bulb glows. Repeat this exact test individually for cells B, C, D, E, and F.
(iii) Conclusion: Cells that cause the test bulb to glow brightly are working. Cells that fail to make the bulb glow (or produce only a barely noticeable filament redness) are dead/discharged.
Examiner & Concept Tip: A standard continuity and voltage load tester isolates working electrochemical cells from exhausted cells.
Q9 • Short Answer LED Polarity & Series Cell Alignment
medium 3 Marks
An LED requires two cells in series to glow. Tanya made a circuit where two cells are placed side by side with similar terminals aligned without cross-connecting wires, and connected to the LED. Will the lamp glow? If not, what must be done to correct the connections?
Model Textbook Solution
No, the lamp will NOT glow in the faulty arrangement.
Corrections required:
1. Series Polarity: The positive terminal of the first cell must be connected to the negative terminal of the second cell using a connecting metal strip or wire.
2. LED Polarity: The longer lead of the LED (anode, positive) must be connected to the free positive terminal of the battery combination, and the shorter lead (cathode, negative) must be connected to the free negative terminal through a switch.
Once these two conditions are met, the closed circuit will have the required 3.0 V potential difference and the LED will illuminate.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Two cells in series produce V_total = V₁ + V₂ = 1.5 V + 1.5 V = 3.0 V, matching an LED's typical forward threshold (~2.0 V to 3.0 V), provided polarities are strictly observed.
Q10 • Short Answer Electric Current Definition
easy 2 Marks
What do you mean by electric current?
Model Textbook Solution
The rate of flow of electric charges across a conductor is known as electric current (I = Q / t). Its SI unit is Ampere (A).
Examiner & Concept Tip: Electric current measures the quantity of electric charge flowing through any cross-section of a conducting wire per second. 1 Ampere equals 1 Coulomb per second (1 A = 1 C·s⁻¹).
Q11 • Short Answer Electric Cell & Current Direction
medium 2 Marks
Define electric cell. What is the direction of electric current in a circuit with an electric cell?
Model Textbook Solution
An electric cell is the simplest source of electric current consisting of a positive terminal (+) and a negative terminal (−). In an external electric circuit, conventional electric current starts from the positive terminal of the cell, passes through the connected equipment/load, and terminates at the negative terminal.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Inside the cell, chemical energy produces an electromotive force that drives electrons out of the negative terminal through the external path into the positive terminal, establishing a conventional current from positive to negative.
Q12 • Short Answer Open Circuit vs Closed Circuit
medium 3 Marks
What is the difference between open circuit and closed circuit?
Model Textbook Solution
1. Open Circuit: A circuit path that contains an unbroken gap/break or an open switch; electric current cannot flow through it; connected electrical devices cannot function.
2. Closed Circuit: A continuous, unbroken conducting path where the switch is closed (ON position); electric current flows continuously through it; connected electrical devices function normally.
Examiner & Concept Tip: A complete conducting loop is essential for continuous charge circulation. When the circuit is broken at any point (open circuit), charge flow ceases throughout the circuit.
Q13 • Short Answer Essential Circuit Components
easy 2 Marks
What are the essential components of an electric circuit?
Model Textbook Solution
The essential components of an electric circuit are:
1. An electric energy source (electric cell or battery),
2. Conducting connecting wires,
3. A controlling device (electric switch/key), and
4. An electrical load/device (such as an electric bulb, resistor, or buzzer).
Examiner & Concept Tip: Without an energy source there is no potential difference; without conducting wires there is no path; without a load energy cannot be utilized; and a switch provides safe control over circuit continuity.
Q14 • Short Answer Electric Fuse Mechanism
medium 2 Marks
What is a fuse?
Model Textbook Solution
A fuse is an electrical safety device connected in series in household circuits to protect appliances and wiring from overcurrent. It contains a thin wire with a low melting point that melts and breaks the circuit when current exceeds a predetermined safe rating, preventing fires and burnouts.
Examiner & Concept Tip: An electric fuse operates on Joule's heating effect (H = I²Rt). If excessive current flows due to short-circuiting or overloading, the wire rapidly heats up, melts, and disconnects the circuit.
Q15 • Short Answer Heating Effect of Electric Current
easy 2 Marks
What is heating effect of the electric current?
Model Textbook Solution
When an electric current passes through a conducting wire or resistive device, the wire or component gets hot due to the dissipation of electrical energy into thermal energy. This phenomenon is known as the heating effect of electric current.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Electrons moving through a resistive conductor collide with the atoms/ions of the metal lattice, converting part of their electrical potential energy into kinetic vibrational thermal energy.
Q16 • Numerical Work Done in Moving Charge
medium 2 Marks
How much work is done in moving a charge of 5 C across two points having a potential difference of 15 V?
Model Textbook Solution
Work done W = 75 J.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Given:
Charge Q = 5 C
Potential difference V = 15 V
Formula: Work done W = V × Q
W = 15 V × 5 C = 75 Joules (J).
Q17 • Short Answer Factors of Heat Production in Conductor
medium 3 Marks
Name the factors on which the heat produced in an electric conductor depends.
Model Textbook Solution
According to Joule's law of heating (H = I²Rt), the heat produced depends on:
(i) The magnitude of the electric current (I) flowing through it (proportional to I²),
(ii) The electrical resistance (R) of the conductor,
(iii) The time duration (t) for which the current flows through the resistor.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Increasing current, resistance, or duration of flow increases the total thermal energy generated in the conductor.
Q18 • Short Answer Material Factors Influencing Heat in a Wire
easy 2 Marks
On what factors does the heat produced in a wire depend?
Model Textbook Solution
The amount of heat produced in a wire depends on its:
1. Material (resistivity of the conductor),
2. Length (resistance increases with length),
3. Thickness / cross-sectional area (thinner wire has higher resistance, hence more heat).
Examiner & Concept Tip: Resistance R is directly proportional to length (l) and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area (A): R = ρ(l / A). Thus thinner, longer wires of high-resistivity material produce more heat for a given current.
Q19 • Short Answer Magnetic Effect of Current
easy 2 Marks
What do you mean by magnetic effect of electric current?
Model Textbook Solution
When an electric current passes through a conducting wire, the wire behaves like a magnet and creates an invisible magnetic field in the surrounding space. This phenomenon is called the magnetic effect of electric current.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Discovered by Hans Christian Oersted in 1820 when a magnetic compass needle deflected when placed adjacent to a current-carrying wire.
Q20 • Short Answer Working of Electric Heater & Iron
medium 2 Marks
How does an electric heater or an electric iron work?
Model Textbook Solution
Electric heaters and electric irons work on the basis of the heating effect of electric current. They contain a coil of high-resistance wire called a heating element (made of Nichrome). When plugged into an electric supply and switched ON, current flows through the element, which becomes red-hot and releases heat without melting.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Nichrome wire has high resistance and a high melting point, enabling it to convert electric energy efficiently into radiant heat without oxidizing easily.
Q21 • Short Answer Overloading vs Short Circuiting
medium 3 Marks
Distinguish between the terms 'overloading' and 'short circuiting'.
Model Textbook Solution
1. Overloading: Occurs when too many electrical appliances of high power ratings are operated simultaneously on a single circuit or socket, causing the total current drawn to exceed the safe current-carrying capacity of the wiring.
2. Short Circuiting: Occurs when the live wire comes into direct physical contact with the neutral wire due to faulty or damaged insulation, reducing circuit resistance to almost zero and causing an instantaneous, extremely large surge of current that can spark fires.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Overloading results from excessive collective load on the circuit, while short-circuiting results from a zero-resistance fault between supply conductors.
Q22 • Short Answer Bar Magnet vs Electromagnet
medium 3 Marks
Write the differences between a bar magnet and an electromagnet.
Model Textbook Solution
Differences:
1. Permanence: A bar magnet is a permanent magnet; an electromagnet is a temporary magnet that functions only when electric current is flowing.
2. Strength: The magnetic strength of a bar magnet is fixed and cannot be changed; the magnetic strength of an electromagnet can be varied by changing the current or the number of coil turns.
3. Controllability: The magnetic properties of a bar magnet cannot be turned OFF; an electromagnet can be switched ON and OFF at will.
Examiner & Concept Tip: An electromagnet's magnetic field is produced by moving charges in a coil around a soft iron core; turning off current instantly dissipates the magnetic domain alignment.
Q23 • Short Answer Uses of Electromagnets
easy 2 Marks
What are the uses of electromagnets?
Model Textbook Solution
Electromagnets are widely used in:
1. Electric bells, buzzers, and electromagnetic relays,
2. Loudspeakers, headphones, and telephone receivers,
3. Electric motors and generators,
4. Industrial cranes for lifting and separating heavy iron scrap,
5. Magnetic Levitation (Maglev) bullet trains and MRI medical imaging machines.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Electromagnets provide controllable, powerful magnetic fields that can be turned on, off, and modulated electronically.
Q24 • Short Answer Electric Fuse Composition & Working
medium 3 Marks
What is an electric fuse made up of? How does it function to prevent a circuit from burning?
Model Textbook Solution
An electric fuse wire is made up of an alloy consisting of approximately 63% tin and 37% lead, possessing a low melting point and high resistance compared to copper wires. When excessive current flows through the circuit, Joule heating (H = I²Rt) rapidly heats the fuse wire above its melting point. The wire melts and breaks, creating an open circuit that immediately halts the flow of current, protecting appliances from damage and preventing electrical fires.
Examiner & Concept Tip: The fuse acts as an intentional sacrificial weak link designed to fail safely before building wiring can overheat.
Q25 • Short Answer Electrical Safety with Sockets (NCERT Exemplar)
medium 2 Marks
Why do we cover plug pin holes which are within the reach of children with cellotape or a plastic cover when not in use? (NCERT Exemplar)
Model Textbook Solution
Children out of curiosity may insert metallic objects or their fingers into unprotected socket holes. Since the human body is a good conductor of electricity, touching live terminals can cause a severe or fatal electric shock. Plastic covers and cellotape are electrical insulators; covering socket holes prevents accidental contact and eliminates the shock hazard.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Insulating covers form a physical barrier preventing human contact with high mains voltage (220 V AC).
Q26 • Short Answer Fuse Ratings in Different Appliances (NCERT Exemplar)
medium 2 Marks
Can we use the same fuse in a geyser and a television set? Explain. (NCERT Exemplar)
Model Textbook Solution
No, we cannot use the same fuse rating in a geyser and a television set. A geyser is a high-power heating appliance (~2000 W) that draws a substantial current (~10 A to 15 A), whereas a television set consumes significantly less power (~100 W) and draws a low current (~1 A to 2 A). If a geyser fuse is used in a TV, it will fail to blow during an electrical fault in the TV, leading to damage. If a TV fuse is used in a geyser, it will blow immediately under normal geyser operation.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Fuses must be calibrated specifically to the normal operating current threshold of the appliance they protect.
Q27 • Short Answer Hazard of Covering Lamps (NCERT Exemplar)
medium 2 Marks
Paheli does not have a night lamp in her room. She covered the bulb of her room with a towel in the night to get dim light. Has she taken the right step? Give one reason to justify your answer. (NCERT Exemplar)
Model Textbook Solution
No, Paheli has not taken the right step. Filament bulbs generate substantial heat due to the heating effect of electric current. Covering the bulb with a towel can cause the towel to overheat and catch fire, creating a serious hazard. In addition, it traps heat and wastes electrical energy. She should use a proper translucent lampshade or a low-wattage night lamp (such as an LED).
Examiner & Concept Tip: Trapping heat on combustible fabrics from incandescent bulbs is a recognized cause of household electrical fires.
Q28 • Short Answer Bulbs & Heating Principles (NCERT Exemplar)
medium 3 Marks
Do all bulbs we use work on the principle of heating effects of electric current? Discuss.
Model Textbook Solution
No, not all bulbs work on the heating effect of electric current. Traditional incandescent filament bulbs work on the heating effect; their tungsten filaments must be heated to white-hot temperatures (~2500°C) to emit light, generating large amounts of unwanted heat and wasting electricity. However, modern fluorescent tube lights, Compact Fluorescent Lamps (CFLs), and Light Emitting Diodes (LEDs) do not rely on high-temperature thermal glow. LEDs operate on electroluminescence (semiconductor electron recombination), converting electrical energy directly into light with minimal heat loss and high energy efficiency.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Filament bulbs are thermal emitters, whereas LEDs and CFLs are non-thermal, energy-efficient photon emitters.
Q29 • Short Answer Electromagnet Coil Turns Comparison (NCERT Exemplar)
medium 2 Marks
Boojho made an electromagnet by winding 50 turns of wire over an iron screw. Paheli also made an electromagnet by winding 100 turns over a similar iron screw. Which electromagnet will attract more pins? Give reason. (NCERT Exemplar)
Model Textbook Solution
Paheli's electromagnet will attract more pins. The strength of the magnetic field produced by an electromagnet is directly proportional to the number of turns of wire in the coil for a given current. Paheli wound 100 turns compared to Boojho's 50 turns, making her electromagnet substantially stronger.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Magnetic field strength B ∝ n·I; doubling the number of turns doubles the total magnetic field contribution of the coil.
Q30 • Short Answer Battery Formation
easy 1 Marks
How can we connect cells to prepare a battery?
Model Textbook Solution
Cells are connected in series by joining the positive terminal (+) of one cell to the negative terminal (−) of the next cell.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Series connection adds the individual electromotive forces to provide a higher cumulative operating voltage.
Q31 • Short Answer Open Circuit Lamp Behavior
easy 1 Marks
Does a bulb glow when the electric circuit is open?
Model Textbook Solution
No, a bulb does not glow when the circuit is open because the conducting loop is broken and no current can flow.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Current requires a closed continuous conducting path to circulate charges through the bulb filament.
Q32 • Short Answer Fused Bulb Non-Illumination (NCERT Exemplar)
easy 1 Marks
A fused bulb does not glow. Why? (NCERT Exemplar)
Model Textbook Solution
A fused bulb does not glow because its internal filament is broken, which breaks the circuit continuity and prevents electric current from flowing.
Examiner & Concept Tip: The broken filament introduces an insulating gap inside the bulb envelope.
Q33 • Short Answer Rapid Cell Discharge (NCERT Exemplar)
medium 1 Marks
In which circuit condition will a cell be used up very rapidly? (NCERT Exemplar)
Model Textbook Solution
The cell will be used up very rapidly when its two terminals are connected directly to each other with a conducting wire without any load resistor (a short circuit).
Examiner & Concept Tip: In a short circuit, resistance is near zero, causing a very high current to flow that consumes the cell's active chemical reagents almost immediately.
Q34 • Short Answer Terminals of an Electric Bulb (NCERT Exemplar)
easy 1 Marks
Which parts of an electric bulb label its two electrical terminals? (NCERT Exemplar)
Model Textbook Solution
The two terminals of an electric bulb are: (1) The metal casing at the base of the bulb, and (2) The metal tip at the bottom center of the base.
Examiner & Concept Tip: These two distinct metal contacts connect to the two lead wires supporting the internal tungsten filament.
Q35 • Short Answer Current in Broken Filament
easy 1 Marks
Is it possible for electric current to flow in a bulb with a broken filament?
Model Textbook Solution
No, it is not possible because the broken filament creates an air gap that breaks the electrical circuit loop.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Air has high dielectric breakdown resistance, preventing low-voltage charge conduction across the break.
Q36 • Short Answer Meaning of the Term 'Battery'
easy 1 Marks
What is the meaning of the term 'battery'?
Model Textbook Solution
A battery is an arrangement of two or more electrochemical cells connected together in series to provide a higher cumulative voltage.
Examiner & Concept Tip: The word battery originates from an array or collection of individual electrochemical cells working in unison.
Q37 • Short Answer Sources of Electricity
easy 1 Marks
Name two common sources of electricity.
Model Textbook Solution
1. Electrochemical cells / dry cell batteries, and 2. Power stations / mains electricity generators.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Dry cells provide portable chemical DC energy, whereas power stations supply AC mains electricity via transmission grids.
Q38 • Short Answer Source of Current in a Torch
easy 1 Marks
What is the source of electric current in a typical torch?
Model Textbook Solution
Electric dry cells (or rechargeable batteries) placed inside the torch casing.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Chemical reactions inside the dry cells supply the electrical potential difference needed to illuminate the torch bulb.
Q39 • Short Answer Material of Bulb Filament
easy 1 Marks
Name the metallic element from which the filament of an electric bulb is made.
Model Textbook Solution
Tungsten (symbol W).
Examiner & Concept Tip: Tungsten has an exceptionally high melting point (3422°C) and emits white light without melting when heated to ~2500°C.
Q40 • Short Answer Electric Circuit Definition
easy 1 Marks
What do you mean by an electric circuit?
Model Textbook Solution
An electric circuit is a continuous, closed conducting path through which electric current can flow from the power source through components and back.
Examiner & Concept Tip: A complete unbroken conducting path is the foundational requirement for electrical current circulation.
Q41 • Short Answer Placement of Key / Switch in a Circuit
easy 1 Marks
In which position can a switch or key be placed in an electric circuit?
Model Textbook Solution
A switch or key can be placed anywhere in the electric circuit loop.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Because current flows sequentially through a series loop, opening the circuit at any point interrupts current everywhere.
Q42 • Short Answer Connecting Cells for a Battery
easy 1 Marks
How can we connect cells to prepare a multi-cell battery?
Model Textbook Solution
By connecting the positive terminal of the first cell to the negative terminal of the second cell, and so on in sequence.
Examiner & Concept Tip: This series polarity alignment adds individual cell voltages: V_total = V₁ + V₂ + ... + V_n.
Q43 • Short Answer Appliances Based on Heating Effect
easy 1 Marks
Name any four household appliances that work on the principle of the heating effect of electric current.
Model Textbook Solution
1. Electric room heater, 2. Electric iron, 3. Electric geyser / water heater, 4. Electric toaster (or electric kettle).
Examiner & Concept Tip: All these appliances contain resistive heating elements (Nichrome) that convert electrical energy into thermal energy.
Q44 • Short Answer MCB Full Form and Nature
easy 1 Marks
What are MCBs?
Model Textbook Solution
MCB stands for Miniature Circuit Breaker. It is an automatic electromagnetic safety switch that trips to the OFF position when current exceeds safe limits.
Examiner & Concept Tip: MCBs have largely replaced traditional fuses in modern household distribution boards because they are resettable without replacing wires.
Q45 • Short Answer Magnet in an Electric Bell
easy 1 Marks
What type of magnet is used in an electric bell?
Model Textbook Solution
An electromagnet (a U-shaped soft iron core wound with insulated copper wire).
Examiner & Concept Tip: An electromagnet is essential because it can be turned on and off rapidly to produce the reciprocating hammer motion.
Q46 • Short Answer Devices Using Magnetic Effect
easy 1 Marks
Name any four devices where the magnetic effect of electric current is used.
Model Textbook Solution
1. Electric bell, 2. Electric motor, 3. Loudspeaker, 4. Industrial scrap-lifting crane (or electromagnetic relay).
Examiner & Concept Tip: These devices use magnetic fields generated by coils of wire carrying electric currents to create mechanical motion.
Q47 • Short Answer Electrical Resistance Definition
easy 1 Marks
What is electrical resistance?
Model Textbook Solution
Resistance is the property of a conductor by virtue of which it opposes the flow of electric charges through it. Its SI unit is the Ohm (Ω).
Examiner & Concept Tip: Resistance results from collisions between moving electrons and vibrating metal lattice atoms.
Q48 • Short Answer Heating Element Definition
easy 1 Marks
What is an 'element' in respect of the heating effect of electric current?
Model Textbook Solution
An 'element' is a tightly coiled wire made of high-resistance, high-melting-point alloy (such as Nichrome) that becomes red-hot and radiates heat when electric current flows through it.
Examiner & Concept Tip: It is the primary active thermal component inside electric irons, heaters, and geysers.
Q49 • Short Answer Effects of Electric Current
easy 1 Marks
What are the primary physical effects produced by an electric current?
Model Textbook Solution
The three primary effects are: 1. Heating effect, 2. Magnetic effect, and 3. Chemical effect.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Electric current produces thermal dissipation (heating), magnetic fields (Oersted effect), and electrochemical reactions (electrolysis).
Q50 • Short Answer Precaution Regarding Lighted Bulb
easy 2 Marks
Why should we never touch a lighted electric bulb connected to the mains?
Model Textbook Solution
A lighted electric bulb connected to the mains becomes extremely hot due to the heating effect of electric current (~2500°C filament radiating high surface heat to the glass). Touching it can cause severe burns to the skin. In addition, if the bulb or socket is faulty, there is a risk of a fatal electric shock.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Substantial electrical energy in incandescent bulbs is converted into thermal radiation, heating the glass envelope to hazardous temperatures.
Q51 • Short Answer Battery Construction and Polarity Alignment
medium 2 Marks
Explain the construction of a multi-cell battery.
Model Textbook Solution
A battery is constructed by connecting two or more electric cells in series. The positive terminal (metal cap) of the first cell is connected to the negative terminal (metal disc) of the second cell using a conducting wire or metal bracket. When cells are placed side by side, a thick wire or metal strip connects the positive terminal of one cell to the negative terminal of the next. The two remaining free terminals serve as the battery's positive and negative terminals.
Examiner & Concept Tip: This series arrangement ensures individual cell voltages add up correctly to power loads requiring higher potential differences.
Q52 • Short Answer Incandescent Lamp vs LED Lamp
medium 2 Marks
What is the difference between an incandescent lamp and an LED lamp?
Model Textbook Solution
1. Operating Principle: An incandescent lamp works on the heating effect of electric current (heating a tungsten filament to white-hot temperatures), whereas an LED works on electroluminescence (semiconductor electron recombination emitting light directly).
2. Energy Efficiency: Incandescent lamps waste most electrical energy as heat with low efficiency (~5%), while LEDs convert nearly all energy into light with very little heat dissipation, consuming far less power and lasting 20–50 times longer.
Examiner & Concept Tip: LEDs are solid-state semiconductor devices, making them far more durable and energy efficient than thermal filament lamps.
Q53 • Short Answer Why Metals Like Copper are Used for Wires
medium 2 Marks
Why are metals like copper used for making electrical connecting wires?
Model Textbook Solution
Copper is used for electrical wiring because:
1. It is an excellent conductor of electricity with very low electrical resistance, ensuring minimal Joule heating energy loss during transmission.
2. It is highly ductile, flexible, and can easily be drawn into thin, durable wires without breaking.
3. It is relatively economical and resistant to corrosion compared to other conductive metals like silver.
Examiner & Concept Tip: High free electron concentration gives copper superior electrical conductivity at reasonable cost.
Q54 • Short Answer Making a Lamp Glow Using a Cell
medium 2 Marks
Explain how an electric lamp can be made to glow using a cell or battery.
Model Textbook Solution
To make an electric lamp glow, a continuous closed circuit loop must be constructed:
1. Connect one insulated copper wire from the positive terminal of the cell to one of the bulb's terminals.
2. Connect a second wire from the negative terminal of the cell through a switch to the other terminal of the bulb.
3. When the switch is placed in the 'ON' position, the circuit loop is completed; electric current flows through the tungsten filament, heating it to incandescence and producing light.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Both bulb terminals must connect to opposite terminals of the power source to form an unbroken conducting loop.
Q55 • Short Answer Working of an Electric Switch
medium 2 Marks
Explain the working of an electric switch in a circuit.
Model Textbook Solution
An electric switch is a simple control mechanism designed to bridge or interrupt a circuit:
- In the 'ON' (closed) position, the switch's internal metallic contacts touch each other, completing the conducting path and allowing current to flow.
- In the 'OFF' (open) position, the metallic contacts are separated by an insulating air gap, breaking the circuit continuity and immediately halting current flow.
Examiner & Concept Tip: The switch provides safe user control over circuit operation without having to physically disconnect wires.
Q56 • Short Answer Why Electric Bulb Gets Hot
medium 2 Marks
Why does an electric bulb get hot if it is switched on for a while?
Model Textbook Solution
An electric bulb gets hot due to the heating effect of electric current (Joule heating). The thin tungsten filament inside offers substantial electrical resistance. As electrons pass through it, their collisions with tungsten atoms convert electrical energy into thermal energy. The filament heats up to over 2500°C to glow white-hot, radiating significant heat into the surrounding inert gas and glass envelope.
Examiner & Concept Tip: According to H = I²Rt, prolonged current flow through the resistive filament generates substantial cumulative heat.
Q57 • Short Answer Factors of Current Heating Effect
medium 2 Marks
What are the factors on which the heating effect of electric current depends?
Model Textbook Solution
According to Joule's Law of heating (H = I²Rt), the heat produced depends on:
1. Current (I): Heat is directly proportional to the square of the current (H ∝ I²).
2. Resistance (R): Heat is directly proportional to the resistance of the conductor (H ∝ R).
3. Time (t): Heat is directly proportional to the duration of current flow (H ∝ t).
Examiner & Concept Tip: Doubling current quadruples heat, while doubling resistance or time doubles heat production.
Q58 • Short Answer Causes of Household Overloading
medium 2 Marks
When does overloading of a household electric circuit occur?
Model Textbook Solution
Overloading occurs when:
1. Too many high-power electrical appliances (such as air conditioners, room heaters, geysers, and irons) are switched on at the same time on the same circuit or plugged into a single socket.
2. An unexpected surge in voltage from the supply grid causes an excessive current draw beyond the safe rated carrying capacity of the domestic wiring.
Examiner & Concept Tip: The total current exceeds the safe rating of the circuit, causing wires to overheat and posing fire hazards.
Q59 • Short Answer Importance of Electric Fuses
medium 2 Marks
What are electric fuses? What is their importance in household circuits?
Model Textbook Solution
An electric fuse is a critical safety device connected in series in the live wire of an electric circuit. It contains a thin wire made of a low-melting-point alloy (tin-lead). Its importance lies in protecting expensive household appliances and building wiring: if a fault causes excessive current (due to short-circuiting or overloading), the fuse wire melts quickly due to Joule heating, breaking the circuit and preventing fires and appliance burnout.
Examiner & Concept Tip: The fuse is a sacrificial protection element engineered to fail before building conductors can ignite.
Q60 • Short Answer Compass Deflection Near Current-Carrying Wire
medium 2 Marks
Why does a magnetic needle get deflected when it is placed near a current-carrying wire?
Model Textbook Solution
A magnetic needle gets deflected because an electric current flowing through a conductor creates an invisible magnetic field in the surrounding region (the magnetic effect of current discovered by Oersted). This magnetic field exerts a magnetic torque on the poles of the magnetic compass needle, forcing it to align with the resultant magnetic field.
Examiner & Concept Tip: The magnetic field produced by moving electric charges interacts directly with the permanent magnetic field of the compass needle.
Q61 • Short Answer Observation Near Current-Carrying Conductor
medium 2 Marks
What happens when a compass needle is brought near a current-carrying wire?
Model Textbook Solution
When brought near a current-carrying wire, the compass needle deflects away from its original North-South direction. If the direction of current in the wire is reversed, the needle deflects in the opposite direction. When the current is switched off, the needle immediately swings back to its natural geographic North-South orientation.
Examiner & Concept Tip: The deflection magnitude and direction correlate directly with the strength and polarity of the induced magnetic field.
Q62 • Short Answer Preparation of an Electromagnet
medium 2 Marks
How are electromagnets prepared?
Model Textbook Solution
An electromagnet is prepared by winding a long coil of insulated copper wire tightly around a soft iron rod or core (such as an iron nail) to form a solenoid. The two ends of the coil are connected to an electric power source (cell or battery) through a switch. When current flows through the coil, the soft iron core becomes strongly magnetized.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Current through the solenoid aligns the magnetic domains of the soft iron core, creating an intense temporary magnetic field.
Q63 • Short Answer Simple Electromagnet Circuit Diagram Description
medium 2 Marks
Describe the setup and diagram of a simple electromagnet working on the magnetic effect of electric current.
Model Textbook Solution
The setup consists of an iron nail around which 50 to 100 turns of insulated copper wire are tightly wound. The ends of the wire are connected in series with a 1.5 V or 9 V battery and a switch/key. When the switch is closed (ON), current flows through the coil and the nail attracts iron paper clips or pins placed nearby. When the switch is opened (OFF), the nail loses its magnetism and the clips drop.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Demonstrates the controllable, on-demand nature of electromagnetic attraction.
Q64 • Short Answer Conductor vs Insulator with Examples
medium 2 Marks
What is the difference between a conductor and an insulator? Provide two examples of each.
Model Textbook Solution
1. Conductor: A material that allows electric current to pass through it easily due to the presence of free valence electrons; has low electrical resistance. Examples: Copper, Aluminium (and Silver, Iron).
2. Insulator: A material that does not allow electric current to pass through it because it lacks free electrons; has extremely high electrical resistance. Examples: Rubber, Plastic (and Glass, Dry Wood).
Examiner & Concept Tip: Conductors facilitate electric current flow, while insulators provide safe physical barriers against current leakage and shock.
Q65 • Long Answer Working of an Electric Torch
hard 5 Marks
How does an electric torch work? Explain its internal components and electrical circuit.
Model Textbook Solution
An electric torch is a portable lighting device powered by dry cells. Its construction and working are as follows:
1. Internal Components:
- Cylindrical Casing: Made of plastic or metal to enclose and protect components.
- Electric Cells: Two or more dry cells arranged in series with the positive terminal of one contacting the negative terminal of the next.
- Metal Spring: Located at the base of the casing, it holds cells firmly in place and acts as a conductor connecting the bottom negative terminal to the circuit.
- Sliding Switch: A control switch with a movable brass strip that completes or breaks the circuit.
- Lamp (Bulb or LED): An incandescent bulb with a tungsten filament or an LED that emits light.
- Reflector: A curved, concave metallic mirror positioned behind the lamp that collects scattered light rays and reflects them forward into a powerful, parallel beam.
2. Electrical Working:
When the sliding switch is pushed forward into the 'ON' position, the internal metal strip slides to touch the base contact of the lamp. This completes the unbroken closed circuit: current flows from the cells' positive terminal, through the lamp filament, through the metal contact strip and switch, through the base spring, and returns to the cells' negative terminal. The filament heats to incandescence and light is beamed forward by the reflector. Sliding the switch back creates an air gap (open circuit), extinguishing the light.
Examiner & Concept Tip: A complete analysis of mechanical, electrical, and optical design elements in portable torchlights.
Q66 • Long Answer Incandescent Lamp Construction and Working
hard 5 Marks
Explain the construction and working of an incandescent lamp.
Model Textbook Solution
An incandescent lamp (electric bulb) consists of the following key features:
1. Construction:
- Glass Envelope: A sealed spherical or pear-shaped glass bulb that protects internal parts and prevents outside air from entering.
- Filament: An ultra-thin coiled wire made of Tungsten. Tungsten is selected because of its exceptionally high melting point (3422°C), high tensile strength, and suitable resistivity.
- Support Wires: Two thick conducting wires (usually made of copper and nickel-iron alloy) that physically hold the tungsten filament in place and conduct electricity to it.
- Base and Terminals: The base of the bulb consists of a threaded metal cap. One support wire connects to the threaded metal casing (terminal 1), while the second connects to an insulated central metal tip at the bottom base (terminal 2).
- Inert Gas Filling: The bulb is evacuated and filled with an inert gas mixture (such as Argon and Nitrogen) at low pressure. This prevents oxidation and rapid evaporation of the white-hot tungsten filament.
2. Working:
When the bulb is connected in a closed circuit, electric current passes through the two base terminals and into the thin tungsten filament. Due to its high resistance and tiny cross-sectional area, Joule heating (H = I²Rt) rapidly raises the filament's temperature to approximately 2500°C. At this intense temperature, the filament glows white-hot, emitting bright visible light along with infrared thermal radiation.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Details the thermal-optical conversion mechanism and protective inert atmosphere of filament lamps.
Q67 • Long Answer Electric Circuit Components & Diagram
hard 5 Marks
What do you mean by an electric circuit? What are the main components of an electric circuit? Draw and describe a diagram of a closed circuit.
Model Textbook Solution
1. Definition of Electric Circuit:
An electric circuit is a continuous, unbroken conducting path through which electric current can flow from the positive terminal of an electric power source to its negative terminal.
2. Main Components:
- Source of Electrical Energy: An electric cell or battery that creates and maintains an electric potential difference.
- Electrical Load: An appliance that converts electrical energy into useful forms, such as an electric bulb (into light/heat), resistor, or motor.
- Controlling Device: A switch or key used to make (close) or break (open) the circuit loop at will.
- Conducting Path: Insulated copper connecting wires that link all elements with minimal electrical resistance.
3. Description of Closed Circuit Diagram:
In a closed circuit diagram, standard symbols are used:
- A battery (alternating long thin line for positive and short thick line for negative terminals) is connected via a solid line (wire) to a switch shown in the closed position (bridged contact line).
- The wire continues through an electric bulb (symbolized by a circle containing a curled filament loop) and returns to the negative terminal of the battery.
- Directional arrows indicate conventional current flowing from the positive terminal (+) through the switch and bulb, returning to the negative terminal (−). Because there are no breaks, current circulates continuously and the bulb glows.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Establishes schematic circuit drafting conventions and closed-loop current continuity.
Q68 • Long Answer Function of Cell Holder and Lamp Holder
medium 4 Marks
What is the function of a cell holder and a lamp holder in an electric circuit?
Model Textbook Solution
1. Cell Holder:
- A cell holder is a molded plastic or wooden compartment fitted with metal terminal clips (or metal springs) designed to hold one or more electric cells securely in place.
- Function: It ensures firm, continuous mechanical and electrical contact with the positive cap and negative disc of the cells. When holding multiple cells, the internal metal connectors link them automatically in proper series polarity (+ to −), providing solderless, accessible terminals for connecting external circuit wires.
2. Lamp Holder (Bulb Holder):
- A lamp holder is a socket fixture that securely houses an electric bulb.
- Function: It holds the bulb upright and provides two isolated metallic spring contacts that touch the bulb's two terminals (the threaded base sleeve and the bottom central tip). This enables safe, convenient, and interchangeable connection of the bulb to external circuit wires without loose or dangerous exposed joints.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Cell and lamp holders provide stable electrical contact, correct polarity alignment, and physical support in experimental circuits.
Q69 • Long Answer Oersted Experiment Demonstration
hard 5 Marks
How can you experimentally demonstrate that an electric current produces a magnetic field?
Model Textbook Solution
The magnetic effect of electric current can be demonstrated using the Oersted experiment as follows:
1. Apparatus Required:
An insulated copper wire, a small magnetic compass needle, an electric cell (1.5 V), a switch/key, and a wooden block or cardboard matchbox tray.
2. Experimental Procedure:
- Place the magnetic compass inside a small shallow cardboard tray.
- Wind several turns of insulated copper wire around the tray over the compass needle.
- Connect the free ends of the wire to an electric cell and a switch in series.
- Keep the switch open (OFF). Observe that the compass needle aligns itself in its natural geographic North-South direction.
- Now, close the switch (ON) so that electric current flows through the wire coil around the compass.
- Observe the compass needle: it immediately twitches and deflects away from the North-South line.
- Open the switch (OFF): current ceases, and the compass needle immediately returns to its rest North-South alignment.
- Reverse the connections at the cell terminals to reverse current direction and close the switch: the compass needle now deflects in the opposite direction.
3. Conclusion:
This deflection proves conclusively that an electric current flowing through a wire produces an invisible magnetic field in its surrounding space, verifying Hans Christian Oersted's discovery (1820).
Examiner & Concept Tip: Direct demonstration of electromagnetic field coupling between moving charge and a permanent magnetic dipole.
Q70 • Long Answer Electromagnet Definition and Applications
medium 4 Marks
What is an electromagnet? Explain its construction and name four modern devices in which it is used.
Model Textbook Solution
1. Definition:
An electromagnet is a temporary magnet consisting of a coil of insulated wire wound around a soft iron core that behaves as a magnet only as long as electric current passes through the coil.
2. Construction:
Take a soft iron core (such as a long iron nail or soft iron rod). Wind insulated copper wire tightly around the core in the form of a helix (solenoid). Connect the two free ends of the coil to a battery and a switch. When current flows, the magnetic field produced by the solenoid magnetizes the soft iron core, creating an intense magnetic field with distinct North and South poles. When the current is switched off, the magnetism vanishes almost completely.
3. Modern Devices Utilizing Electromagnets:
- Electric bells and buzzers,
- Industrial cranes for lifting and sorting heavy iron scrap,
- Loudspeakers and telephone earpieces,
- Magnetic Levitation (Maglev) bullet trains and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) medical scanners.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Electromagnets offer unique advantages over permanent magnets: high controllable strength and instant on/off switching.
Q71 • Long Answer Working of an Electric Bell
hard 5 Marks
Explain the construction and working of an electric bell with a detailed step-by-step mechanism.
Model Textbook Solution
An electric bell operates on the magnetic effect of electric current. Its construction and working are as follows:
1. Construction:
- Electromagnet: A U-shaped soft iron core wound with insulated copper wire.
- Soft Iron Armature: A movable iron strip mounted on a flexible flat spring positioned directly in front of the electromagnet poles.
- Hammer: A small metal ball attached to the free end of the armature strip.
- Gong: A hollow hemispherical metallic cup mounted near the hammer.
- Contact Screw: An adjustable screw with a pointed contact that rests lightly against the back of the armature when the circuit is at rest.
- Battery and Push Button: Connected in series with the electromagnet and contact screw assembly.
2. Working Mechanism:
- Step 1: When the push button switch is pressed, the circuit is completed and current flows from the battery through the contact screw, through the armature, and through the electromagnet coils.
- Step 2: The energized electromagnet immediately attracts the soft iron armature towards its poles.
- Step 3: As the armature moves forward, the hammer attached to its end strikes the metal gong, producing a loud ringing sound.
- Step 4: However, the forward movement pulls the armature away from the contact screw tip, breaking the circuit at the contact screw point.
- Step 5: Breaking the circuit stops the current flow; the electromagnet loses its magnetism instantly and can no longer attract the armature.
- Step 6: The flexible spring pulls the armature back to its original resting position, re-establishing contact with the screw tip.
- Step 7: Re-establishing contact completes the circuit once again, energizing the electromagnet to pull the armature forward anew. This rapid make-and-break cycle repeats continuously, causing the hammer to strike the gong repeatedly as long as the button is held down.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Classic mechanical-electromagnetic self-interrupting circuit mechanism producing continuous acoustic strikes.
Q72 • Long Answer Testing Conductors vs Insulators Experiment
medium 4 Marks
How will you experimentally determine whether a given unknown object is an electric conductor or an insulator?
Model Textbook Solution
To test whether an unknown object is an electric conductor or an insulator, construct a simple continuity tester as follows:
1. Circuit Assembly:
- Connect an electric dry cell (1.5 V), an electric torch bulb mounted in a holder, and two insulated copper connecting wires.
- Leave the two terminal wire ends (Wire A and Wire B) exposed with stripped bare copper tips.
- Verify that the tester works by touching tip A directly to tip B: the circuit completes and the bulb glows brightly.
2. Testing Procedure:
- Place the unknown test sample on an insulated surface.
- Press tip A firmly against one point of the object and tip B against a separated point on the object.
3. Observation & Conclusion:
- Case 1 (Conductor): If the bulb glows, electric current is successfully passing through the object from tip A to tip B. The material contains free charge carriers and is an electrical conductor (e.g., metal key, aluminum foil, iron nail, copper coin).
- Case 2 (Insulator): If the bulb does not glow, electric current cannot pass through the object. The material has high electrical resistance with no free charges and is an electrical insulator (e.g., plastic ruler, rubber eraser, glass strip, dry wood, paper).
Examiner & Concept Tip: Standard empirical two-terminal continuity test protocol.
Q73 • Numerical Current Calculation (I = Q / t)
medium 2 Marks
If 600 C of electric charge flows through a circuit, what will be the current (in A) drawn by the filament of an electric bulb in 10 minutes?
Model Textbook Solution
Current I = 1 A.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Given:
Total charge Q = 600 C
Time t = 10 minutes = 10 × 60 seconds = 600 s
Formula: Current I = Q / t
I = 600 C / 600 s = 1.0 A.
Q74 • Numerical Potential Difference Calculation (V = W / Q)
medium 2 Marks
The work done in moving a 20 C charge across two points is 400 J. The potential difference between these two points is x V. Find the value of x.
Model Textbook Solution
x = 20 V.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Given:
Work done W = 400 J
Charge Q = 20 C
Formula: Potential difference V = W / Q
V = 400 J / 20 C = 20 V.
Therefore, the value of x is 20.
Q75 • Numerical Resistance from Ohm's Law (R = V / I)
medium 2 Marks
A bulb draws a current of 0.22 A from a 220 V mains source. The resistance of the filament of the bulb is x Ω. What is the value of x?
Model Textbook Solution
x = 1000 Ω.
Examiner & Concept Tip: Given:
Potential difference V = 220 V
Current I = 0.22 A
Formula: According to Ohm's Law, R = V / I
R = 220 V / 0.22 A = 1000 Ω.
Therefore, x = 1000.

Draw in your notebook the symbols to represent the following components of electrical circuits: connecting wires, switch in the 'OFF' position, bulb, cell, switch in the 'ON' position, and battery.
Model Textbook Solution
